title: Hot Water Can Freeze Faster Than Cold Water
description:
A teenager in Tanzania stumbled onto this by accident in 1963, and physicists still don't fully agree on why it happens -- or exactly when it actually does.

#shorts #sciencefacts #physics #didyouknow
sources: PBS NOVA's "The ice cream that changed physics"

scenes.text: In 1963, a teenager in Tanzania made a batch of ice cream, and accidentally stumbled onto something physicists still can't fully agree on.

Erasto Mpemba skipped letting his boiled milk cool before freezing it, just to beat his classmates to the last ice tray. An hour later, his was already frozen -- while theirs, started from cold, was still liquid.
His own physics teacher told him that wasn't possible. Years later, a visiting physicist took the question seriously, tested it properly, and published the results.
It turns out Aristotle, Francis Bacon, and Descartes had all separately noted the same strange thing, centuries earlier -- nobody had ever properly explained it.

It's now called the Mpemba effect, and it's still genuinely disputed. Some controlled experiments have reproduced it. Others, including a well known 2016 study, found it depends heavily on exactly how and where you measure the temperature.
Nobody's saying hot water always freezes faster. The honest answer is that under very specific conditions, it sometimes can -- and scientists still don't fully agree on why.
Would you have believed hot water could freeze before cold water?
